episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Thursday, May seventh, twenty twenty-six. And here's who is innovating in higher education today.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Leading off today's Innovation Pulse, thousands of schools and universities have lost access to the Canvas learning management system after a cyberattack during finals week. CBS News reports that the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for breaching Instructure, the company behind Canvas. The attackers exploited a vulnerability in Free-For-Teacher accounts and posted a ransom message on login pages across the country. Students at Penn State, the University of Wisconsin-Madison, Columbia, UCLA, Northwestern, and the University of Chicago report being locked out of course materials, grades, and assignments. Penn State canceled all tests at its Pollock Testing Center Thursday night and Friday. The University of Texas at San Antonio postponed finals. The hackers claim nearly nine thousand schools worldwide were affected, with billions of private messages and records accessed. Instructure says it is working to restore full service, and school districts including Spokane, Washington are reassuring parents about data security. Canvas serves more than thirty million active users at more than eight thousand institutions and manages grades, assignments, lecture videos, and course communications.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In research news, a new study from Cornell and Carnegie Mellon universities found that A.I. tools are reshaping the college admissions essay in ways admissions offices may not expect. Researchers analyzed tens of thousands of application essays at a selective college and found that essay language became measurably more similar across all applicants after A.I. writing tools became widely available in twenty twenty-two. Students who received application fee waivers were more likely to use A.I. in their essays than other applicants. And lower-income students who used A.I. faced higher rejection rates than higher-income students who also used A.I. The findings, published by Inside Higher Ed, raise new questions about equity as A.I. assistance becomes a standard part of the application process.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Turning to workforce development, the national nonprofit Advance CTE unveiled a new five-year vision for career and technical education at its spring meeting in Oxon Hill, Maryland. Education Week reports that the organization released a document titled The Connected Path, describing each student's educational journey as a connected series of experiences rather than isolated steps between school and the workforce. The announcement comes as career and technical education enrollment jumped ten percent in one year, from seven point eight million to eight point six million students nationwide, according to the U.S. Department of Education. At Riverside High School in Greer, South Carolina, students in an introduction to A.I. class are already presenting projects that use A.I. to boost agricultural productivity. The vision document calls for stronger coordination between K through twelve schools, community colleges, and employers to create what it describes as a co-designed system that works for learners and industry equally.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Meanwhile, community college faculty now have a free path to A.I. training through a new partnership between IBM and the National Applied A.I. Consortium. The consortium, founded in twenty twenty-four with National Science Foundation funding and led by Miami Dade College, has partnered with IBM's SkillsBuild platform to deliver customized A.I. learning for community college educators across the country. Faculty and staff can access more than one thousand courses covering A.I., cloud computing, cybersecurity, and data science through a structured pathway from foundational literacy to advanced hands-on labs. The collaboration supports IBM's goal of skilling thirty million people globally by twenty thirty, including two million learners in A.I. by the end of this year.

<break time="1.0s"/>

And court documents filed in the Elon Musk and Sam Altman litigation have revealed that the University of Michigan invested twenty million dollars in OpenA.I. during one of the company's earliest funding rounds. Business Insider reports that the university set a target redemption amount of two billion dollars on that stake. The investment arrived before Microsoft committed billions and before ChatGPT launched in November twenty twenty-two. OpenA.I. closed a one hundred and twenty-two billion dollar funding round in March at a valuation of eight hundred and fifty-two billion dollars. If the university holds its position through a public offering, the return could exceed one hundred to one, making it one of the most successful technology bets by a university endowment in recent history.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Thank you for joining us. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

leadStory.headline: Canvas Cyberattack Reveals Growing Vulnerability of Concentrated EdTech Infrastructure
leadStory.summary: The Canvas learning management system returned online Friday after a cyberattack forced thousands of schools and universities offline during finals week, revealing vulnerabilities in educational technology infrastructure that has become concentrated among a few major providers. CBS News reports that the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for breaching Instructure, the company behind Canvas. The attack exploited Free-For-Teacher accounts, prompting the company to temporarily shut down these accounts while restoring full service. The timing created chaos as students lost access to course materials, assignments, and lecture videos needed for final exams. Affected institutions included Penn State, the University of Wisconsin-Madison, Columbia University, UCLA, Northwestern University, and the University of Chicago. Penn State canceled all tests at its Pollock Testing Center and rescheduled affected exams for the following week. Some schools postponed finals scheduled for Friday while others worked to set up alternative assessment methods for students who could not access the platform during the outage. The hackers claimed nearly 9,000 schools worldwide were affected, with billions of private messages and records accessed. Public school districts like Spokane reassured parents that student data remained secure despite the breach. Instructure worked to restore service throughout the day as institutions scrambled to communicate with students through email and social media about exam logistics. The company restored access to Free-For-Teacher accounts after implementing additional security measures. Canvas handles assignment submissions, grade tracking, and course communications for educational institutions across K-12 and higher education. The incident follows other recent cyberattacks on educational platforms serving multiple institutions.

quickHits.headline: Study Finds Lower-Income Students More Likely to Use A.I. in College Admissions Essays
quickHits.summary: A Cornell and Carnegie Mellon study found that students who received application fee waivers were more likely to use A.I. in their college admissions essays than other applicants. Inside Higher Ed reports that the researchers analyzed tens of thousands of essays submitted to an unnamed selective institution over four years. Lower-income students who used A.I. faced higher rejection rates than higher-income students who also used A.I. Lead author Jinsook Lee, a Ph.D. candidate at Cornell, noted that higher-income students have access to better versions of A.I. tools plus counselors and essay coaches who understand how to use A.I. effectively. Lee pointed out that lower-income students might only access free-tier ChatGPT rather than premium versions, affecting output quality. The researchers found that essay language became more similar across all applicants after A.I. tools became widely available in 2022. Co-author AJ Alvero, a Cornell sociology professor, said A.I. may be pushing applicants toward the same template.

quickHits.headline: CTE Enrollment Surges 10 Percent as High Schools Add A.I. Classes
quickHits.summary: Career and technical education enrollment jumped 10 percent in one year, from 7.8 million to 8.6 million students, as high schools add A.I. courses to their programs. Education Week reports that at Riverside High School in Greer, South Carolina, students in an Introduction to A.I. class present A.I.-powered projects designed to boost agricultural gains. The growth comes as CTE programs expand technology offerings to match workforce demands. Walter Ecton, an assistant professor at the University of Michigan and CTE expert, said it is not reasonable to expect CTE teachers to keep up with A.I. developments on their own. Ecton said the field needs real professional development and support. Advance CTE Executive Director Kate Kreamer said things are moving faster than ever with generative A.I. and there is uncertainty about what work will look like in five years. The enrollment data comes from the U.S. Department of Education. More than 40 national organizations have signed on to support efforts to strengthen CTE connections with career opportunities.

quickHits.headline: Miami Dade College Forms National Consortium After Faculty Complete A.I. Training
quickHits.summary: Miami Dade College formed the National Applied A.I. Consortium after faculty at the college completed A.I. training through IBM SkillsBuild. EdTech Innovation Hub reports that Antonio Delgado Fornaguera, Vice President of Innovation and Tech Partnerships at Miami Dade, founded the consortium to bring the training model to community colleges across the United States. Faculty at Miami Dade worked through more than 1,000 courses covering A.I., cloud, cybersecurity, and data science. The training moved educators from foundational A.I. literacy to advanced concepts with hands-on labs using open-source A.I. models. Faculty gained access to data science tools and analytical platforms used in industry. The program prepares instructors to teach A.I. concepts to students entering technical fields. The consortium makes these resources available to faculty at other community colleges. IBM reported that the partnership supports its goal of training two million people in A.I. by end of 2026 as part of a commitment to skill 30 million people globally by 2030.

quickHits.headline: Court Documents Reveal University of Michigan's $20 Million OpenA.I. Stake
quickHits.summary: Court documents filed in the Elon Musk and Sam Altman litigation show that the University of Michigan invested $20 million in OpenA.I. and set a target redemption amount of $2 billion. Business Insider reports that the investment details emerged from an exhibit in the ongoing lawsuit over OpenA.I.'s governance. The university's endowment managers invested before Microsoft and before ChatGPT's release in November 2022. The document does not specify the exact terms of Michigan's stake, but the university set its target return at one hundred times the initial investment. OpenA.I.'s valuation has increased dramatically since ChatGPT launched. The stake became public only through court filings in the litigation between Musk and Altman. Michigan invested during one of OpenA.I.'s early fundraising rounds. University endowments typically invest in a mix of stocks, bonds, and alternative assets to fund operations and scholarships. The $20 million stake is one of the largest known university investments in a private A.I. company.
